name: ChaCha20-BLAKE3
baseline: XChaCha20-Poly1305 and AES-256-GCM (via RustCrypto's pure-Rust crates, not OpenSSL or libsodium)
workload: Single-core AEAD encrypt throughput at message sizes 64 B, 1 KB, 64 KB, 1 MB, and 10 MB
claimed_speedup: ~1.3x vs XChaCha20-Poly1305 at 64 KB (2,153 vs 1,636 MB/s), ~2x at 1-10 MB (3,297-3,353 vs 1,654-1,664 MB/s) (derived from page data); but 2-5x SLOWER than both XChaCha20-Poly1305 and AES-256-GCM at 64 B-1 KB message sizes
tradeoffs: New, non-standardized AEAD construction (not NIST/IETF standardized like GCM/Poly1305); requires a 24-byte nonce; committing-AEAD design adds security (full context commitment) but is slower than both baselines for small messages
caveats: First-party benchmark on the author's own repo/blog, single run, no statistical repetition. The RustCrypto comparison implementations are explicitly labeled 'non-optimized' by the author, who states an optimized ChaCha20-BLAKE3 build would be ~30% faster still. The author also says they were 'surprised how slow AES-256-GCM' was on AES-NI-capable hardware, suggesting that comparison arm may not reflect a properly hardware-accelerated AES-GCM. No compiler/rustc version or build flags stated. Not benchmarked against OpenSSL or libsodium directly.
found_via: Hacker News: "Show HN: ChaCha12-BLAKE3: Secure and Fast committing AEAD Encryption for Any CPU" (item 44825449, 2025-08-07); repo has since moved to github.com/skerkour/chacha20-blake3

name: stdx-go ChaCha20 (Go simd/archsimd)
workload: ChaCha20 keystream/encrypt throughput at 64 B-1 MB inputs, single core, amd64 (AVX2/AVX-512) and arm64 (NEON)
claimed_speedup: amd64: up to 7.5x at 1 MB (7,517.67 MB/s simd vs 1,005.23 MB/s stdlib) (derived from page data, headline '7.5x faster'); arm64: no gain, ~97% of stdlib speed (1,349.27 vs 1,390.28 MB/s at 1 MB)
hardware: amd64: AMD EPYC Zen5 family (model unspecified); arm64: host CPU unspecified
tradeoffs: Relies on Go's experimental `simd`/`simd/archsimd` packages (GOEXPERIMENT=simd), not part of stable Go; author explicitly marks the code 'NOT production-ready'; implements raw ChaCha20 only, not the ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD; arm64 SIMD path gives no real speedup over stdlib
caveats: First-party blog benchmark by the library's own author. CPU stated only as a family ("AMD EPYC Zen5"), not an exact model, and the arm64 host CPU is not named at all, so it falls short of full Tier-A hardware disclosure. Benchmarks Go's own stdlib chacha20 package, not OpenSSL/libsodium.
found_via: Hacker News: "SIMD ChaCha20" -> "7.5x faster encryption in Go with the new 'simd' and 'simd/archsimd' packages" (item 49362187, 2026-08-19)

name: rscrypto (AEAD suite: AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, XChaCha20-Poly1305, AEGIS-256, Ascon-AEAD128)
baseline: AES-256-GCM / ChaCha20-Poly1305 / XChaCha20-Poly1305, benchmarked against a mix of external crates (RustCrypto aes-gcm/chacha20poly1305, ring, aws-lc-rs, dryoc) rather than OpenSSL or libsodium directly
workload: AEAD encrypt/decrypt throughput across varying input sizes on an 8-host CI matrix (x86_64 AMD/Intel, aarch64 Graviton, ppc64le, s390x, riscv64, plus Windows x86_64)
claimed_speedup: "Fastest-external" geomean (best competing crate per case) (derived from page data): AES-256-GCM 1.83x (94/36/46 win/tie/loss over 176 rows), XChaCha20-Poly1305 1.43x (173/3/0), Ascon-AEAD128 1.39x (136/39/1), AEGIS-256 1.23x (81/65/30), ChaCha20-Poly1305 1.12x (75/101/0)
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.98.1 stable (x86_64/aarch64/Windows CI hosts); rustc 1.99.0-nightly (ppc64le/s390x/riscv64 hosts); exact `cargo bench`/target-cpu flags not detailed in the overview doc
hardware: AWS EC2 CI runners: c8a.2xlarge (AMD x86_64), c8i.2xlarge (Intel x86_64), c9g.2xlarge (Graviton aarch64), plus native ppc64le/s390x/riscv64 runners and c8a/c8i.2xlarge Windows
tradeoffs: Pure-Rust, avoids OpenSSL/libsodium/C-FFI by design (no_std/WASM friendly); "fastest-external" ratios pick whichever competitor crate happened to be fastest per row, so the specific rival beaten varies case to case rather than being one fixed named baseline; some other primitives in the same suite lose to competitors (e.g. ECDSA-P384 sign 0.70x)
caveats: Self-reported CI benchmark campaign from the project's own repo/GitHub Actions runs, not an independent third-party suite. The OVERVIEW.md itself documents prior methodology corrections for AEAD/workload-identity issues, indicating the numbers have shifted between campaigns. None of the tested competitors (RustCrypto aes-gcm/chacha20poly1305, ring, aws-lc-rs, dryoc) is literally OpenSSL or libsodium; dryoc is a pure-Rust reimplementation of libsodium's API, not the libsodium C library itself, so this is not a direct beat of the named category incumbents.
found_via: Hacker News: "Show HN: Rscrypto 0.4 treats constant-time as a release gate" (item 48478270, 2026-06-10)
